title: POC Weekly Sync - Quality Eval & Regression
summary: Weekly POC sync to review quality eval results from the pilot, discuss regressions on recent prompt changes, agree on guardrail adjustments and next steps for a focused benchmark run. SE presented scoring breakdown; customer raised concerns about sensitive PHI leakage and latency tradeoffs for higher-quality prompts.

Customer to provide 20 additional edge-case prompts by 2025-04-17
SE to share sanitized example outputs and attack-case doc by 2025-04-18
Schedule a dedicated latency/cost tradeoff call the week of 2025-04-21 if needed

Alicia Gomez | Deliver 20 edge-case prompts and three annotated failing examples | 2025-04-17
Samir Khan | Confirm allowable PHI handling and KMS requirements, send security checklist | 2025-04-18
header:
Date: 2025-04-15
Time: 10:00 AM PDT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Alicia Gomez (Cascadia PM), Dr. Nikhil Rao (Cascadia ML Lead), Samir Khan (Cascadia Security), Priya Desai (Data Analyst)
Recording: Yes
Notes: Transcript auto-generated by Fireflies
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna run through the quality eval results from the pilot. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Alicia Gomez: Alicia here, thanks.
[00:06] Dr. Nikhil Rao: Nikhil on the line.
[00:08] Samir Khan: Samir.
[00:09] Maya Patel: Maya from Redwood.
[00:11] Jordan Lee: Cool. Maya, you had the slides and the scoring sheets?
[00:15] Maya Patel: Yep, I'll share screen — ok jumping to the eval dashboard. Quick reminder: we ran the 1k prompt test set, plus your 150 annotated examples, and compared baseline prompts vs. the tuned prompts we pushed last Wednesday. Scoring buckets: correctness (0-5), hallucination penalty (-2 to 0), safety (binary check for PII/PHI), and adherence to template (0-3).
[00:41] Maya Patel: Results summary: tuned prompts improved average correctness from 3.6 to 4.0, overall score +9%. However we saw a regression on the cardiology subset — average correctness down 0.4 points, and two cases where PHI-like strings were included in the completion.
[01:00] Dr. Nikhil Rao: Can you repeat the PHI cases? Were those patient identifiers or just clinical terms?
[01:05] Maya Patel: In the two flagged outputs the model surfaced a sequence that looked like a sample MRN pattern — it's likely hallucinated token sequences that match numeric patterns. They were not real PHI from your dataset but still unacceptable.
[01:17] Samir Khan: That's a big risk for us. We're also constrained by data residency and audit trails.
[01:27] Jordan Lee: Understood. To be clear, these were in the test outputs only, not in logs tied to customers. But we treat this seriously. Maya, what guardrails did we have on the run?
[01:36] Maya Patel: We had basic PII redaction post-processing disabled for the eval to measure raw model behavior. We did run the contextual PII detector in reporting only. For the next run we recommend enabling both the detector and a conservative filter for MRN/SSN-like regex patterns, plus a lower temperature and a prompt clamp that includes explicit "do not output patient identifiers" instruction.
[02:00] Priya Desai: If we enable the filter, will it increase false positives and hurt correctness metrics?
[02:06] Maya Patel: Possibly, yes; you could see a slight dip in correctness if the filter masks tokens we would otherwise accept. But safety constraints are higher priority for production. We can tune scoring weights to reflect that.
[02:18] Alicia Gomez: On the cardiology subset regression — do you think it's prompt-related, or model variant? We switched from 2.7B quantized to 7B last week for that bucket.
[02:30] Maya Patel: Good catch. The change to 7B likely increased hallucination propensity on narrow, specialized prompts; we saw longer completions with more invented specifics. For the cardiology prompts, the baseline 2.7B answered more conservatively. We can run an A/B: tuned prompts on both model variants and log differences.
[02:47] Dr. Nikhil Rao: We'd prefer the more conservative model if it reduces risky fabrications. Latency matters but not at the cost of PHI hallucination.
[02:56] Jordan Lee: That tracks — tradeoff conversation. We can schedule a focused performance vs. safety analysis.
[03:02] Maya Patel: Also, we observed a handful of template-adherence failures — some completions dropped the required 'recommendation' bullet. Likely prompt mismatch on a few edge cases. The action is to extend the prompt set with those edge cases.
[03:16] Priya Desai: I uploaded three failing examples in the shared folder earlier.
[03:19] Jordan Lee: Great, we'll fold those in.
[03:22] Maya Patel: Operationally, for the next eval run we propose: enable PII detector + regex filters, lower temperature from 0.9 to 0.3 for safety-critical prompts, run on both 2.7B quantized and 7B variant, and weight safety higher in the score calc (safety 30%, correctness 40%, template 20%, hallucination penalty 10%).
[03:44] Alicia Gomez: Sounds reasonable. How long will that rerun take?
[03:47] Maya Patel: For 1.15k prompts across two model variants it'll be ~3-4 hours compute; we can kick it off today and have results and csv by 2025-04-22.
[03:58] Samir Khan: Also need to confirm where the logs are stored during the eval. We need audit logs to live in your VPC-proxy for dedicated/private, or at minimum be able to export them to our S3.
[04:09] Jordan Lee: We're able to configure logs to your S3 bucket for the POC; for Dedicated/Private we'll ensure audit logs go to your KMS-protected storage. We'll send a note with the exact retention and KMS details.
[04:20] Samir Khan: Please include SOC2 scope and whether the PII detector is part of the runtime or post-processing.
[04:26] Maya Patel: It's post-processing today in the hosted eval pipeline, but for Private we can enable an in-line runtime detector if you want lower surface area. We'll document options.
[04:36] Jordan Lee: Nikhil, any more concerns on scoring or success criteria?
[04:40] Dr. Nikhil Rao: I want to see per-class precision/recall for the cardiology bucket and examples of false positives from the safety filter. Also would like a short QA rubric so our clinical SMEs can validate outputs easily.
[04:51] Maya Patel: We can provide per-class confusion matrices and the automated rubric we used for human annotation. That will help reproduce.
[04:57] Alicia Gomez: Timeline-wise, if we get the adjusted eval on 22nd and see 95%+ safety pass and acceptable correctness, we can move to a 2-week pilot extension with dedicated capacity for heavier throughput testing.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: Excellent. Any blockers on Redwood side?
[05:13] Maya Patel: Just need the 20 edge-case prompts and confirmation on whether to run both model variants — we recommend both.
[05:20] Priya Desai: I'll compile the 20 prompts by tomorrow EOD.
[05:24] Jordan Lee: Perfect. Final recap: Redwood will run the guarded eval (PII detector + regex filters, lower temp) across 2.7B quantized and 7B and return results by 2025-04-22, include per-class metrics and examples. Customer will send additional prompts and share policy constraints. Samir will confirm security checklist answers.
[05:43] Samir Khan: One more quick note — for production we'll want KMS integration and an SLA on purge of logs that contain any sensitive tokens.
[05:51] Jordan Lee: Noted. We'll include that in the security doc.
[05:55] Maya Patel: I'll open a ticket with the eval config and attach the scoring spreadsheet and the sample failing outputs.
[05:59] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and the next run. Meeting adjourned.
[06:05] End of recording.
